newsitem.title: USA: US group urges renegotiation of Canada lumber pact.
newsitem.headline: US group urges renegotiation of Canada lumber pact.

text.p: The National Association of Homebuilders said Tuesday that the U.S. government should immediately renegotiate the U.S.-Canada lumber agreement signed earlier this year.

The association said at a news conference that the agreement is "creating havoc in lumber markets, sending prices to near record levels" and adding more than $2,000 to the cost of building a typical single-family home.
The group said that the bilateral agreement has caused lumber prices to rise 36 percent, or $126 per thousand board feet, from early April, when the agreement was announced.

"If prices hold at current levels, we are looking at a $2 billion lumber tax on the projected 1.1 million single-family homes that will be built in the next 12 months," association president Randy Smith said.

Smith called on the Clinton administration to immediately renegotiate the pact. He also called on Rep. Phil Crane (R-Ca.), chairman of the trade subcommittee of the House Ways and Means Committee, to conduct hearings to investigate.
The five-year agreement sets a 14.7 billion board feet per year limit on shipments of lumber from British Columbia, Quebec, Ontario and Alberta to the United States.
Shipments above that level pay import tariffs of $50 to $100 per 1,000 board feet.
